National Strategy for Financial Inclusion (NSFI): 2025-30 The NSFI 2019-2024 had set forth the vision and key objectives of the financial inclusion policies in India to help expand and sustain the financial inclusion process at the national level through a broad convergence of action involving all the stakeholders in the financial sector. Continuing the journey, NSFI: 2025-30 envisions upscaling the financial inclusion efforts towards seamless and effective access to a bouquet of formal financial services, coupled with financial literacy, consumer awareness and customer protection. Released by - Financial Inclusion and Development Department (FIDD), Reserve Bank of India

# Page 4^page=4
National Strategy for Financial Inclusion (NSFI): 2025-30

# Page 5^page=5
CHAPTER – I - NATIONAL STRATEGY FOR FINANCIAL INCLUSION (NSFI) 2019-24: A RETROSPECT • The strategy was created after taking inputs and suggestions from the Government of India and various financial sector regulators, such as: o Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) o Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) o Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) • It also included consultations with specialised institutions and market participants, including: o National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) o National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) o Commercial Banks • The document was formally released by Shri M K Jain, Deputy Governor, RBI at the High Level Meeting on Financial Inclusion for the North East region convened at Agartala on January 10, 2020.

# Page 6^page=6
CHAPTER – I - NATIONAL STRATEGY FOR FINANCIAL INCLUSION (NSFI) 2019-24: A RETROSPECT • An inclusive financial system promotes stability, integrity, and fair growth, which NSFI aimed to achieve through 6 strategic pillars and 18 milestones. By emphasising last-mile delivery, banking access was ensured within 5 km for 99.9% of the 1.21 lakh identified villages/hamlets (500 households), and multiple measures were taken to strengthen the Business Correspondent (BC) network for last-mile access.

# Page 7^page=7
Assessment of Progress in Achievement of NSFI Milestones: • Over five years, regulators worked on encouraging safe and responsible financial innovation by testing new ideas through the Regulatory Sandbox and bringing practical digital solutions to the last mile. • On the demand side, financial inclusion improved as every block in the country was covered through Centres for Financial Literacy (CFL), and NCFE created easy, customised financial literacy modules for different groups. • Banking outlets in villages increased from 5.97 lakh (March 2019) to 15.98 lakh (March 2024), and basic savings bank deposit accounts rose from 57.42 crore to 70.59 crore over the same period. • During the strategy period, the Reserve Bank introduced 2 indices in 2021 — the Digital Payments Index (DPI) to measure digital payment adoption, and the Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index) to assess overall financial inclusion. • The DPI increased significantly from 153.47 (March 2019) to 445.50 (March 2024). • The FI-Index improved from 49.9 (2019) to 64.2 (2024), with the Access sub-index rising from 67.5 to 79.3, Usage sub-index from 38.7 to 55.5, and Quality sub-index from 52.6 to 65.8.

# Page 8^page=8
CHAPTER-II - STATE OF FINANCIAL INCLUSION IN INDIA All major parameters such as - per capita bank accounts, cards, mutual fund assets under management, bank deposits, and credit etc, have grown steadily over the past 5 years with no negative trends, showing a gradual expansion of the financial system, along with consistent growth in mutual fund assets under management (MF-AUM) and rising current deposits. Banking infrastructure per lakh population improved sharply, with fixed-point business correspondents rising from 30.1 to 85.6, while bank branches stayed around 12.5 per lakh population and ATMs remained stable at 17–18 per lakh population.

# Page 9^page=9
Supply Side Impediments to Financial Inclusion: Demand Side Impediments to Financial Inclusion: Most BC outlets mainly handled remittances and cash services, while products like insurance, micro- pension, loans, overdrafts, KCC were available only at select outlets, leading to uneven service access in areas fully dependent on BCs. In the household segment, personal loans, education loans, and home loans were the top 3 credit facilities in demand, yet about 50% of aspirants had unmet credit needs. Lack of awareness about the procedure, unavailability of nearby bank branch, and lack of collateral were cited as top three impediments in that order, for inability to get credit. The absence of a prescribed minimum standard set of BC services led to poor standardisation, making it difficult to manage customer expectations and monitor service delivery. Information asymmetry - lack of awareness about availability, cost, and use of financial services, and difficulty in understanding information because of language or literacy barriers. The survey showed that most BCs did not display service fees, and concerns existed about unauthorized or unaccounted upfront charges, in addition to bank-built transaction charges. Among those without insurance or pension products, awareness of their need was low; awareness about schemes like PMSBY, PMJJBY, PMFBY, and APY ranged between 30-35%. Low representation of women BC agents reduced inclusivity and outreach. Near-universal ownership (96%) of bank account, but irregular income limited active usage. Around 16% of the respondents used informal sources of credit mostly for small ticket loans, with its share being higher in rural areas. In general, people may have relied upon informal sources of credit due to ease, timeliness, and convenient access.

# Page 10^page=10
CHAPTER – III - VISION OF NSFI (2025-30): AN INCLUSIVE FINANCIAL SYSTEM TOWARDS WELLBEING OF PEOPLE Equitable: The access infrastructure should be available across the geographic strata in a reasonably homogeneous manner. Responsible: Financial service providers should ensure that their products and services do not manipulate or limit customers’ free choice, interests, or suitability needs, and do not leave customers worse off in economic, behavioural, or social terms. Suitable: Financial products and services should match customers’ needs, financial situation, and understanding, with customised options available so people can choose what suits them best. Affordable: Basic financial services like basic accounts, savings and investment accounts, small remittances, and small digital payments should be provided free of cost, while other services should be priced affordably, keeping service costs in mind.

# Page 11^page=11
CHAPTER – III - VISION OF NSFI (2025-30): AN INCLUSIVE FINANCIAL SYSTEM TOWARDS WELLBEING OF PEOPLE Financial inclusion, as above, with the involvement of all stakeholders improves financial safety, financial security, financial resilience, and financial discipline of individuals (households) and micro-enterprises.

CHAPTER – III - VISION OF NSFI (2025-30): AN INCLUSIVE FINANCIAL SYSTEM TOWARDS WELLBEING OF PEOPLE • The financial inclusion (FI) ecosystem is a coordinated network of stakeholders working together to improve people’s well- being through financial safety, security, resilience, and discipline.

# Page 15^page=15
CHAPTER – IV - NSFI (2025-30): STRATEGIC OBJECTIVES AND ACTION POINTS Five strategic and synergised objectives, collectively referred to as Panch-Jyoti, comprising 47 specific action points, which are aimed at helping to elevate the state of financial inclusion in the country: 1. Improving the availability and use of Equitable, Responsible, Suitable, and Affordable Bouquet of Financial Services to achieve Financial Safety and Financial Security for households and micro enterprises. 2. Adopting Gender-Sensitive Approach for Women-led Financial Inclusion and Differentiated Strategies for Improving Financial Resilience of Households, especially for the Underserved and Vulnerable segments. 3. Synergizing Livelihood, Skill Development and Support Ecosystem and its linkages with Financial Inclusion. 4. Leveraging Financial Education as a tool for promoting Financial Discipline. 5. Strengthening the Quality and Reliability of Customer Protection and Grievance Redressal Measures. The NSFI 2025-30 timeline is aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, adopted by 193 UN Member States in Sept 2015 and effective from Jan 1, 2016. The agenda’s principles of “Leave No One Behind” and holistic development closely match NSFI’s outcome-focused financial inclusion goals aimed at improving people’s well-being.c:

# Page 16^page=16
CHAPTER – IV - NSFI (2025-30): STRATEGIC OBJECTIVES AND ACTION POINTS

# Page 17^page=17
CHAPTER-V – Monitoring and Measurement Mechanism Supply Side Measurement: • Data collection should fully cover all formal financial institutions involved in the financial inclusion ecosystem. • Data should be collected at the district level, with gender and age-wise breakup, to assess regional, gender, and age-related differences in access and usage; key banking datapoints should be placed in the public domain. • Customer data captured by financial service providers should include income level, education, occupation, and purpose, to support better analysis and policy design. • Common and harmonised definitions should be developed for terms such as Vulnerable Consumers and Migrants, for consistent use across the financial sector. • While the current FI-Index measures progress at the national level, a disaggregated FI-Index should be developed—preferably at the State/UT level—and during NSFI 2025–30, a new, broader FI-Index series with State/UT-level data should be constructed and published. Financial inclusion indicators are grouped under Access, Usage, and Quality, with breakdowns by geography and demographics; while supply-side assessment uses regulatory and other available data, demand-side assessment requires surveys and studies to understand on-ground quality and enablers.

# Page 18^page=18
CHAPTER-V – Monitoring and Measurement Mechanism Demand Side Measurement - Conduct of Studies/Surveys • Along with supply-side data, demand-side measurement through surveys and focus groups is needed to identify barriers to access, usage, and quality of financial inclusion, especially at the last mile. • A user-focused approach helps reveal gaps between needs and services, last-mile delivery bottlenecks, regional gaps, and changing preferences. Way Forward: Financial inclusion works best when it is linked with financial education, customer protection, skills, livelihoods, entrepreneurship, and market access through joint efforts, helping improve people’s financial safety, security, resilience, and discipline.

Q.1) With reference to the “Panch-Jyoti” framework under the National Strategy for Financial Inclusion (NSFI) 2025–30, consider the following statements: 1. Panch-Jyoti represents five strategic and synergised objectives supported by a total of 47 specific action points. 2. One of its objectives explicitly links the provision of equitable, responsible, suitable, and affordable financial services with the achievement of financial safety and financial security. 3. Gender-sensitive financial inclusion under Panch-Jyoti is limited to improving women’s access to credit through self-help groups. 4. Financial education is envisaged as an instrument to promote financial discipline rather than merely financial awareness. Which of the statements given above are correct? A. 1 and 2 only B. 1, 2 and 4 only C. 2 and 3 only D. 1, 3 and 4 only E. 1, 2, 3 and 4 Answer: ?

Q.2) The objective of financial inclusion is to provide ______________access to formal financial services—such as savings, payments, remittances, credit, investments, insurance, and pension—across all socio-economic and geographic groups, supported by strong financial literacy, consumer awareness, and customer protection. With the involvement of all stakeholders, financial inclusion strengthens financial safety, security, resilience, and discipline of individuals, households, and micro-enterprises. Which of the following should fill the blank? A. Equitable, universal, subsidised and mandatory B. Inclusive, affordable, profitable and innovation-led C. Responsible, inclusive, technology-driven and risk-free D. Equitable, responsible, suitable and affordable E. Regulated, centralised and standardised Answer: ?
